summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would change responsibility for defamatory social media posts and create ways for Australians to obtain information about people who posted potentially defamatory material.
Australian page administrators would be protected from liability for others' posts, while service providers would be treated as publishers of material posted in Australia.
Providers could obtain a conditional defence through complaint handling and disclosure requirements, with contact details released only with the poster's consent or a court order.
changes: Courts could order disclosure of whether material was posted in Australia and, where applicable, the poster's contact details.
Courts could refuse disclosure orders where a poster's safety might be at risk.
Specified overseas providers would have to establish an Australian company as their nominated agent.
The Attorney-General could intervene in relevant proceedings and authorise payment of applicants' reasonable legal costs.
summary.affected: Social media users, Australian page administrators, service providers, defamation claimants and courts would be affected.

speeches.speaker: Paul Fletcher
speeches.brief: The government introduced the Social Media (Anti-Trolling) Bill to protect page owners from defamation liability for third-party posts, make social media platforms liable as publishers, and create mechanisms to unmask anonymous trolls via a complaints scheme and court orders, while requiring foreign platforms to establish an Australian nominated entity.

speeches.speaker: Mark Dreyfus
speeches.brief: The speaker argued the Social Media (Anti-Trolling) Bill 2022 was a publicity stunt introduced after the Senate had risen, ensuring it could not pass before the election, and criticised the government for scheduling only 10 House sitting days in four months. They noted the bill’s title was misleading, calling it a defamation measure that could worsen trolling, and referenced a 1,200-day delay on a national anticorruption commission, as well as evidence from Sonya Ryan and barrister Sue Chrysanthou SC.
